meta.title: Who really said "In war, events of importance are the result of trivial causes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Caesar really wrote it — De Bello Civili III.68 — but the neat 8-word line is a condensed variant translation, not his literal wording.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In war, events of importance are the result of trivial causes'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Caesar (Civil War III.68), but the tidy English — and the tidy Latin — are later condensations of his actual sentence.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 100–44 BC · Roman general, statesman & author of the war Commentaries
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Caesar’s: it condenses a sentence from his own memoir De Bello Civili (The Civil War), Book III, 68 — Latin “… parvis momentis magnas rerum commutationes efficit”, on how fortune, above all in war, turns great outcomes on tiny hinges. The neat eight-word English, though, is a condensed ‘variant translation’ ↗, not the wording of any standard scholarly edition.

source.excerpt: But fortune, which has great influence in affairs generally and especially in war, produces by a slight disturbance of balance important changes in human affairs; as happened then.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section as a variant translation of The Civil War, Book III, 68.
The passage’s Latin — “Sed fortuna … parvis momentis magnas rerum commutationes efficit” — sits in Caesar’s own text ↗.
A. G. Peskett’s public-domain 1914 Loeb translation ↗ renders it “… produces by a slight disturbance of balance important changes in human affairs.”
source.excerptNote: A. G. Peskett’s Loeb translation (1914) of the sentence at Civil War III.68. The circulating eight-word line — “In war, events of importance are the result of trivial causes” — tightens this same passage into an aphorism.

sourceLink.text: Caesar, The Civil War III.68 (Loeb, 1914) at Penelope

source.rightsNote: Caesar’s Latin original (De Bello Civili III.68, c. 45 BC) and A. G. Peskett’s Loeb translation of 1914 are both long in the public domain. The exact popular eight-word English wording, however, is an unattributed condensation whose specific translator and date could not be identified, so its copyright status as shown is left open.

author.heading: Caesar, in his own words
author.metaLine: 100–44 BC · Roman general, statesman & author of the war Commentaries
author.bio: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose campaigns and civil war reshaped the Republic. He was also his own historian: his terse third-person Commentaries on the Gallic and civil wars are prized as models of Latin prose. The reflective aside quoted here comes from that self-authored account of the war against Pompey.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake — the idea and the source are real. What has drifted is the packaging: both the tidy English and a tidy Latin version that circulate are later condensations, not Caesar’s literal words.

items.who: A condensed paraphrase, not a literal translation
items.why: Caesar’s sentence is longer and hedged around fortuna; standard translations read “fortune … produces by a slight disturbance of balance important changes in human affairs.” The eight-word aphorism is a variant rendering ↗.

items.who: A spurious rewording that spreads online
items.why: A neat Latin form — “in bello parvis momentis magni casus intercedunt” — is often passed off as Caesar’s original, but his actual text ↗ reads “parvis momentis magnas rerum commutationes efficit.”

misattribution.truthLine: The reflection is authentically Caesar’s, from his own memoir of the civil war (Civil War III.68 ↗); it is the crisp English and Latin sound-bites that are later inventions.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Caesar wrote the line as an author reflecting on his own campaign against Pompey. It arrives at De Bello Civili III.68, amid the hard fighting around Dyrrhachium, where a local reverse could easily have turned decisive — the very kind of small hinge the sentence is about.

The aphorism’s afterlife owes as much to translators and quote books as to Caesar: stripped of its Latin qualification around fortuna (fortune), it became a portable maxim about how great events pivot on trivial causes.
detailsBody: Standard Loeb and Wikiquote citations place the sentence at Book III, 68; some Latin editions (e.g. The Latin Library) number the surrounding chapters slightly differently. The wording and Latin are the same passage.
context.pull: Fortune, especially in war, turns great changes on very small hinges.
